title: Not to Be Trusted
core: All four flag something that fails inspection: a claim, a document, a set of figures, a person's motives. They differ on two axes. First, **certainty**: two of them only raise an eyebrow — the verdict is pending — while two deliver the verdict outright. Second, **what has gone wrong**: whether the thing merely attracts doubt, or whether it has no legitimate basis, or whether it has a legitimate-looking surface over rotten reasoning.

words.nuance: The only one that can face **inward**: *I'm dubious* describes the doubter, not the doubted. Outward, it is the mildest of the four — a raised eyebrow with full deniability, and the only one that runs ironic (*the dubious distinction of the highest crash rate*).

Strictly **passive** — it says what we think of the thing, never what the thing thinks. It attaches to what is under assessment (data, evidence, timing, a witness's motives) and is the professional's dry hedge: cooler than *fraudulent*, far more damning than *unproven*. Also the only one that doubles as a noun and verb.

A **verdict on origin**: the thing has no legitimate standing at all — a forged deed, a correlation that isn't there. Crucially it needs **no liar**; bad sampling produces spurious results with nobody deceiving anyone. Where the others question a thing, this one refuses to engage with it.

A **verdict on surface**: unlike the others, it concedes the thing *is* attractive — it passed the first look. It aims almost exclusively at **reasoning**, not objects or people, and implies the speaker did the second look. The insult is that the falsehood was well-tailored.

exam_note: The classic trap is swapping **spurious** and **specious**: spurious = no basis (bad pedigree), specious = plausible basis that fails (bad logic that looks good) — and only **specious** requires the thing to be superficially persuasive.
